subject: Fluid Mechanics + Heat Transfer
summary: a full revision of Fluid Mechanics (stability of floating bodies, kinematics, radial flow and Bernoulli, angular momentum, dimensional analysis, laminar film flow, boundary-layer separation, minor losses) and Heat Transfer (conduction with heat generation, fins, Prandtl number, black-body radiation, shape factors, ε-NTU heat exchangers and the overall heat transfer coefficient)

questions.text: A solid wooden cylinder of diameter D and height H (specific gravity 0.6) floats in water with its axis vertical, as shown. The minimum ratio D/H for it to float stably in this position (round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: A floating body is stable if its metacentric height GM = BM − BG > 0, with BM = I/V (I = second moment of the waterplane area, V = displaced volume).
Immersed depth h = 0.6H. G is at H/2 and B at h/2 = 0.3H above the base, so BG = 0.5H − 0.3H = 0.2H
Exam tip: A tall thin cylinder floats on its side; it can float upright only if it is wide enough for BM to exceed BG.

questions.text: A two-dimensional flow has the velocity field u = x², v = −2xy. The flow is
solution: Concept: Continuity (incompressible): ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0. Rotation: ωz = ½(∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y).
∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 2x − 2x = 0: the flow is incompressible.
∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = −2y − 0 = −2y ≠ 0 (except on y = 0): the flow is rotational, so no velocity potential exists.
Answer: (C) incompressible and rotational.
Exam tip: A stream function exists for every 2-D incompressible flow; a velocity potential exists only if the flow is also irrotational.

questions.text: Water flows radially outward at 0.01 m³/s between two parallel horizontal discs 5 mm apart, as shown. Neglecting losses, the rise in pressure from a radius of 0.1 m to a radius of 0.3 m (in kPa, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Continuity in radial flow: Q = 2πrbV, so V ∝ 1/r. Bernoulli (same level): p₂ − p₁ = ½ρ(V₁² − V₂²).
Exam tip: The flow slows down as it spreads out, so the pressure rises outward (the discs are pushed apart less at the rim than near the centre).

questions.text: A lawn sprinkler, shown in plan, has two equal arms of radius 0.2 m, each ending in a 5 mm diameter nozzle pointing tangentially. The total flow is 0.4 litres per second. The torque needed to hold the sprinkler stationary is about
solution: Concept: Angular-momentum equation for a control volume: T = Σ ṁ V r for the tangential jets.
0.41 N·m counts only one nozzle.
Exam tip: If the sprinkler is free to rotate at ω, the absolute jet speed becomes V − ωr, and the torque falls to zero when ωr = V (no friction).

questions.text: The discharge Q over a triangular (V) notch depends on the head H over the notch, the acceleration due to gravity g and the notch angle θ (viscosity and surface tension neglected). Dimensional analysis gives
solution: Concept: Rayleigh's method: Q = C ga Hb f(θ), θ being dimensionless.
[L³T⁻¹] = [LT⁻²]<sup>a</sup>[L]<sup>b</sup> → T: −1 = −2a → a = ½; L: 3 = a + b → b = 5/2
So Q = √g H5/2 f(θ): (D). The V-notch formula Q = (8/15) Cd √(2g) tan(θ/2) H5/2 has exactly this form.
Exam tip: Option (A) is H3/2√g, the form for a rectangular notch per unit width (Q/L).

questions.text: Oil (density 900 kg/m³, dynamic viscosity 0.2 Pa·s) flows steadily in laminar regime as a film 3 mm thick down a wide plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², the velocity at the free surface of the film (in mm/s, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: In a falling film, gravity along the plane is balanced by viscous shear; with zero shear at the free surface, u(y) = (ρg sinθ/μ)(hy − y²/2).
At y = h: u<sub>s</sub> = ρg sinθ h²/(2μ)
Check: flow per metre width q = ρg sinθ h³/(3μ) = 1.99 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s, mean velocity = 66.2 mm/s = (2/3)u<sub>s</sub>; Re = ρVh/μ ≈ 0.9, laminar.
Exam tip: The film profile is half of the plane-Poiseuille parabola, so the mean is 2/3 of the surface velocity.

questions.text: In a boundary layer on a curved surface, flow separation occurs at the point where
opts: the pressure gradient dp/dx becomes zero
the velocity gradient (∂u/∂y) at the wall becomes zero in a region of adverse pressure gradient
the boundary-layer thickness becomes equal to the radius of curvature
the free-stream velocity reaches its maximum value
questions.ans: (B) the velocity gradient (∂u/∂y) at the wall becomes zero in a region of adverse pressure gradient
solution: Concept: In an adverse pressure gradient (dp/dx > 0) the slow fluid near the wall is decelerated until it stops and reverses.
Separation point: wall shear τ<sub>w</sub> = μ(∂u/∂y)<sub>y=0</sub> = 0; downstream of it (∂u/∂y)<sub>wall</sub> < 0 (reversed flow).
dp/dx = 0 marks the point of minimum pressure (maximum free-stream velocity), which lies upstream of separation: (B).
Exam tip: Separation can never occur in a favourable pressure gradient (dp/dx < 0); a turbulent boundary layer resists separation longer than a laminar one.

questions.text: Water flows through a sudden contraction from a large pipe into a smaller pipe in which the velocity is 3 m/s. The coefficient of contraction at the vena contracta is 0.62. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², the head loss due to the contraction (in m, round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: The loss in a sudden contraction is mainly the expansion loss from the vena contracta (velocity V₂/Cc) to the full pipe: hL = (1/Cc − 1)² V₂²/(2g).
Exam tip: With Cc ≈ 0.62 the loss coefficient is about 0.375; for a very large area ratio it is often rounded to 0.5V²/2g (sharp entrance).

questions.text: The steady temperature distribution in a plane wall 0.1 m thick (k = 40 W/m·K) is T = 200 − 500x − 2000x² (T in °C, x in m from the left face). The volumetric heat generation rate in the wall is
solution: Concept: Steady 1-D conduction with generation: d²T/dx² + q̇/k = 0, so q̇ = −k d²T/dx².
Check: the flux leaving the right face, −k dT/dx at x = 0.1 = 40 × (500 + 400) = 36 000 W/m², minus that entering at x = 0 (40 × 500 = 20 000 W/m²) = 16 000 W/m² = q̇L. ✔
Exam tip: 8.0 × 10⁴ comes from forgetting that the second derivative of 2000x² is 4000, not 2000.

questions.text: A long copper pin fin (k = 380 W/m·K) of 4 mm diameter has an insulated tip; h = 20 W/m²·K. The shortest fin length for which it transfers 99 % of the heat of an infinitely long fin of the same section (in mm, round off to the nearest whole number) is ______
solution: Concept: Insulated-tip fin: Q = √(hPkA) θb tanh(mL); infinite fin: Q = √(hPkA) θb. Their ratio is tanh(mL).
Exam tip: Beyond mL ≈ 2.5–3 extra fin length adds almost nothing, which is why copper fins are kept short.

questions.text: The Prandtl numbers of common fluids near room temperature, arranged in increasing order, are
opts: liquid mercury < air < water < engine oil
air < liquid mercury < water < engine oil
liquid mercury < water < air < engine oil
engine oil < water < air < liquid mercury
questions.ans: (A) liquid mercury < air < water < engine oil
solution: Concept: Pr = ν/α compares momentum diffusion with heat diffusion.
Liquid metals conduct heat very well (large α): Pr ≈ 0.01–0.03 for mercury.
Gases: Pr ≈ 0.7 (air). Water: Pr ≈ 7 at 20 °C. Oils (very viscous): Pr ≈ 100–10 000.
Order: (A) mercury < air < water < engine oil.
Exam tip: δt/δ ≈ Pr−1/3: the thermal boundary layer is much thicker than the velocity layer for liquid metals and much thinner for oils.

questions.text: A furnace whose inner walls are at 1200 K has a small circular sight-hole of 20 mm diameter in its wall. The surroundings are at 300 K. Treating the hole as a black body and taking σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴, the net rate of radiation loss through the hole (in W, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: A small opening in a large isothermal cavity absorbs almost all radiation entering it, so it behaves as a black body at the cavity temperature.
Exam tip: Black-body cavities are used as radiation standards; the T⁴ term of the 300 K surroundings changes the answer by less than 0.4 %.

questions.text: A long cylinder of diameter D is placed centrally inside a long duct of square cross-section of side 2D, as shown. The shape factor from the inner surface of the duct to the cylinder is
solution: Concept: All radiation leaving the convex cylinder (1) strikes the duct (2): F₁₂ = 1. Reciprocity: A₁F₁₂ = A₂F₂₁.
Per unit length: A₁ = πD, A₂ = 4 × 2D = 8D
Exam tip: 0.785 = π/4 would result from taking the duct perimeter as 4D; always draw the geometry before using reciprocity.

questions.text: In a counter-flow heat exchanger, oil (heat capacity rate 1.5 kW/K) enters at 140 °C and is cooled by water (heat capacity rate 6 kW/K) entering at 20 °C. The product UA is 2.25 kW/K. The outlet temperature of the oil (in °C, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: ε-NTU method for counter flow: ε = [1 − e−NTU(1−Cr)]/[1 − Cre−NTU(1−Cr)].
C<sub>min</sub> = 1.5 kW/K (oil), C<sub>r</sub> = 1.5/6 = 0.25, NTU = UA/C<sub>min</sub> = 2.25/1.5 = 1.5
Q = εC<sub>min</sub>(T<sub>h,in</sub> − T<sub>c,in</sub>) = 0.7350 × 1.5 × 120 = 132.3 kW
Oil outlet = 140 − 132.3/1.5 = 51.8 °C (water leaves at 20 + 132.3/6 = 42.1 °C; profiles below)
Exam tip: When outlet temperatures are unknown, use ε-NTU; LMTD would need trial and error.

questions.text: In a thin-walled tube heat exchanger, the inside and outside heat transfer coefficients are 1000 W/m²·K and 250 W/m²·K (wall resistance and fouling negligible). To raise the overall heat transfer coefficient, which change is more effective, and what does U become?
opts: Doubling the inside coefficient; U = 333 W/m²·K
Doubling the inside coefficient; U = 222 W/m²·K
Doubling the outside coefficient; U = 222 W/m²·K
Doubling the outside coefficient; U = 333 W/m²·K
questions.ans: (D) Doubling the outside coefficient; U = 333 W/m²·K
solution: Concept: For a thin wall 1/U = 1/hi + 1/ho; the larger resistance controls U.
Doubling h<sub>i</sub>: 1/U = 0.0005 + 0.004 → U = 222 W/m²·K
Doubling ho: 1/U = 0.001 + 0.002 → U = 333 W/m²·K: (D)
Exam tip: Always attack the side with the lower h (usually the gas side); that is also where fins are added.
